working_title: Scotland's Moray Firth Golf Coast: A Practical Guide to Playing Nairn, Lossiemouth and Beyond
angle: The Moray Firth coastline sits between Inverness and Aberdeen and is genuinely under-visited by UK golfers who tend to leapfrog it for Royal Dornoch or St Andrews. This guide makes the case for the region as a self-contained golf trip, covering the anchor courses (Moray Golf Club at Lossiemouth, Nairn) and the affordable character courses that make the itinerary worth building around (Hopeman, Cullen Links).
research_notes:
- The Moray Firth sits roughly midway between Aberdeen and Inverness on Scotland's north-east coast, making it a natural stopping point for driving golf itineraries through the Highlands
- Region noted for a favourable microclimate: courses reportedly playable almost year-round, with October flagged as a strong shoulder-season option for reduced crowds
- Moray Golf Club, Lossiemouth (est. 1889): two 18-hole links courses — Old Course laid out by Old Tom Morris, New Course designed by Sir Henry Cotton; both ranked among Scotland's best; course starts and finishes in the town of Lossiemouth (similar to St Andrews in that regard); closing hole widely regarded as one of the finest in Britain
- Nairn Golf Club (est. 1887): championship links founded by Robert B Finlay, extended by Archie Simpson, Old Tom Morris and James Braid; has hosted the Walker Cup, Curtis Cup, Amateur Championship and Women's Amateur Championship; part of the Highland Golf Links partnership alongside Royal Dornoch and Castle Stuart; Golfshake lists guide green fees at £230 per round for the Championship Course (high season) — confirm with club before including in post
- Nairn Dunbar Golf Club: a neighbouring, less prominent option that offers online booking and is notably more affordable than Nairn Golf Club
- Hopeman Golf Club: extended from 9 to 18 holes in 1985; described as one of the most demanding links courses in Moray; fairways guarded by gorse and broom; signature 12th hole (par 3, 'The Prieshach') plays down into Clashach Cove roughly 150 feet below the tee; Paul Lawrie (Honorary President) has called it probably the best par 3 he has ever played; Sky Golf has voted it one of the best par 3s in Scotland; dolphins visible in the Firth from the tee; clubhouse known as The Mashie Niblick, serves Cullen Skink and homemade food; noted as family-friendly and affordable
- Cullen Links: originally laid out by Old Tom Morris in 1870 as 9 holes; extended to 18 by local architect Charlie Neaves; nestled beneath red sandstone cliffs in harbour town of Cullen; just over 4,600 yards, making it the shortest of the world's recognised true links courses; ten par 3s in the layout; holes 12 and 13 play over an 80ft rock formation called Boar Crag; now on the Old Tom Morris Trail; described as quirky, scenic, and great value
- The Moray Firth Golf Pass exists (morayfirthgolf.co.uk) and offers discounts across local courses — worth directing readers to check it
- Elgin Golf Club (inland, est. 1906): 6,458 yards, par 69, scratch 71; regarded as one of the finest inland courses in north Scotland — useful contrast/addition for a multi-day itinerary
- Fortrose & Rosemarkie: 20 minutes from Inverness, good arrival-day option; chance of spotting Moray Firth dolphins from the course
- Dolphins (bottlenose) are a genuine draw along the whole Firth coastline and visible from several courses — worth noting as an aside
- Driving logistics: Inverness airport is the natural arrival point; Lossiemouth/Elgin area is a sensible base; courses spread along the coast allow a logical driving route rather than doubling back
- No invented prices beyond the Golfshake guide figure for Nairn Championship Course (£230 high season — flagged as guide price only); all other green fee specifics should be described in general terms or readers directed to each club's website
